title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $Y$ be a Young diagram colored with respect to $\mathcal{C}_n$. Then the 
  partition associated to $Y$ is an $n$-core iff $Y$ contains no significant 
  arrows as defined in \cite{Maclagan_Smith_2010}.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $Y \subset \mathbb{N}^2$ be a Young diagram colored by $\mathcal{C}_n$ and 
  set $a_n = a_0$. Then 
  $$2B = 2a_0 - \sum_{i = 0}^{n - 1} (a_i - a_{i + 1})^2$$
  where $B$ is equal to the number of border strips which can be 
  removed from $Y$ before obtaining an $n$-core.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
$Y$ is an $n$-core diagram if and only if
  $2a_0 = \sum_{i = 0}^{n - 1} (a_i - a_{i + 1})^2$

label: GFlatLimit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{GFlatLimit}
 There exists a unique $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G)$ such that 
 $\varrho(\Xi_t) \simeq \rho$ for all closed $t \in T$.
 \begin{proof}
  Note the claim is local on $T$ and hence we may assume $T = \operatorname{Spec}(A)$. 
  Let $I$ denote the ideal corresponding to $\Xi$ in $A[x,y]$.
  Next fix a choice of $t \in T$ and let $m_t \subset A$ 
  denote the corresponding maximal ideal. Pass to the 
  localization $M_t = M \otimes_A A_{(m_t)}$. From the definition of 
  $\rho = \varrho(\Xi_t)$ it follows there is an isomorphism of 
  representations $M/ m_t M \simeq \rho$. By Nakayamas lemma we may lift a 
  basis of $M/ m_t M$, $\{f_i'\}$, to a minimal generating set of $M_t$ denoted 
  as $\{f_i\}$. Clear denominators so that we may assume 
  $f_i \in \operatorname{im}(M \rightarrow M_t)$ and thus also assume $\tilde{f}_i$
  is a lift of $f_i$ for each $i$. Now consider 
  $\sum_i A \tilde{f}_i \subset M$. 
    
  As $A \rightarrow A_{(m_t)}$ is injective and $M$ is flat it follows 
  $M \rightarrow M_t$ is injective as well. In particular for a relation of 
  the form
  \begin{equation*}
    a_1 \tilde{f}_i + ... + a_m \tilde{f}_m = 0
  \end{equation*}
  upon pushing forward and using freeness of $M_t$ necessarily each 
  $a_i = 0$. In other words $\sum_i A \tilde{f}_i$ is a free $A$-module.
  Hence by comparing lengths and using $\bigoplus_i A_t f_i \simeq M_t$ 
  we may prove $M \simeq \bigoplus_i A \tilde{f}_i$.
  Now factor $A$ from the last direct sum so
  \begin{equation*}
    M \simeq \bigoplus_i A \tilde{f}_i \simeq A \otimes \bigg(\bigoplus_i \mathbb{C} \tilde{f}_i \bigg)
  \end{equation*}
  As $A \rightarrow A_{(m_t)}$ is an injective $\mathbb{C}$-linear map, the action of $G$ 
  fixes the coefficients. Each $f_i$ is a lift so that
  \begin{equation*}
    \bigoplus_i \mathbb{C} \tilde{f}_i \simeq \bigoplus_i \mathbb{C} f_i \simeq \bigoplus_i \mathbb{C} \tilde{f}_i' \simeq \rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G)
  \end{equation*}
  Hence $M \simeq A \otimes_{\mathbb{C}} \rho$ for some $\mathbb{C}$-linear injection 
  $1 \otimes \rho \rightarrow M$. To finish up choose an arbitrary 
  maximal ideal $m_s \subset A$ so $A/m_s \simeq \mathbb{C}$ and calculate the 
  isomorphisms of $\mathbb{C}$-modules
  \begin{equation*}
    \varrho(\Xi_s) = M_s \simeq M \otimes_A A/m_s \simeq A/m_s \otimes_{\mathbb{C}} \rho \simeq \rho
  \end{equation*}
  For the last isomorphism we have used $A \rightarrow A/m_s$ is a 
  $\mathbb{C}$-algebra homomorphism and hence is injective on $\mathbb{C}$. Finally we applied 
  a simple dimension count.
 \end{proof}

label: FlatnessCrit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{FlatnessCrit}
    Fix an integral scheme $T \in Sch/k$. Define $G$ to act trivially on $T$ 
    in the product $\mathcal{X}_T$. Let $\mathfrak{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}_T$
    be a family of 0 dimensional substacks and let $\Xi \subset \mathbb{A}_T^2$
    be the associated family of subschemes.
    Then $\mathfrak{Z} \rightarrow T$ is flat iff there exists a 
    unique $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G)$ such that $\varrho(\Xi_t) \simeq \rho$ for 
    all closed $t \in T$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G)$ and $h_{\rho}$ be the corresponding Multigraded 
  Hilbert Polynomial. Then there is a natural isomorphism of 
  schemes $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]} \simeq \operatorname{Hilb}_G^{h_{\rho}}$.
  \begin{proof}
    To begin, the functor $H_G^h$ is defined on $\mathbb{C}$-algebras which by 
    the $\operatorname{Spec}$ construction is equivalent to the category of affine 
    $\mathbb{C}$-schemes. As affine schemes form a base of the Zariski site 
    of $Sch/\mathbb{C}$ it follows $H_G^{h_{\rho}}$ may be extended to a sheaf; 
    $H_G^{h_{\rho}}$ will also be used to refer to the extension. 
    Clearly $\operatorname{Hilb}_G^{h_{\rho}}$ still represents the extension. 
    As such to prove the claim it suffices to show there is a natural 
    isomorphism $\mathcal{H}ilb_{\rho}(T) \simeq H_G^{h_{\rho}}(T)$
    for an arbitrary affine $\mathbb{C}$-scheme $T = \operatorname{Spec}(A)$. Moreso as both 
    $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}, \operatorname{Hilb}_G^{h_{\rho}}$ are quasiprojective 
    schemes it also suffices to only consider when $A$ is noetherian.
    
    For a given morphism $f: T \to \operatorname{Hilb}_G^{h_{\rho}}$ let $I$ denote the 
    family of ideals arising from the universal property of fine moduli spaces.
    Next form the isotypic decomposition $\rho = \sum_{g \in G} a_g \chi(g)$. 
    From the definitions we have 
    \begin{equation*}
      A[x,y]/I \simeq \bigoplus_{g \in G} A[x,y]_g/I_{g}
    \end{equation*}
    The assertion $h_{\rho}$ is constant on $\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C})$ when 
    extended to families amounts to the requirement 
    $$h_{\rho}((A[x,y]/I)_{g} \otimes_A m ) = a_g$$ 
    for all maximal $m \subset A$. Importantly as $G$ acts trivially on $A$ 
    it follows $\deg(a) = 0$ for all scalars so the isomorphism
    $(A[x,y]/I) \otimes_A m \simeq (A/m)[x,y]/I$
    is compatible with the group structure and the $G$-grading. Thus 
    there is an isomorphism of graded rings 
    \begin{equation*}
      (A[x,y]/I) \otimes_A m \simeq \bigoplus_{g \in G} (A/m)[x,y]_g/I_{g}
    \end{equation*}
    In total, the constancy of $h_{\rho}$ is equivalent to 
    requiring the length of $(A/m)[x,y]_g/I_{g}$ to be independent
    of the choice of maximal ideal $m$. 
    
    Set $\Xi = \operatorname{Spec}(A[x,y]/I)$
    and let $\mathfrak{Z}$ denote the corresponding family of stacks. 
    It is easy to verify that 
    being an admissible ideal implies $I$ is a $G$-ideal 
    with respect to the given action. Moreso as $\sum_i a_i$
    is equal to both the colength of $I_t$ and $\deg(\rho)$ it follows each 
    fiber of $I$ is a finite colength ideal. As $T$ is an integral 
    noetherian scheme we may use that $\Xi$ has constant representation 
    type and Proposition \ref{FlatnessCrit} to show 
    $\mathfrak{Z}$ is flat over $T$. As this is compatible with 
    base change the association $I \to \mathfrak{Z}$ defines a 
    functor of sheaves $H_G^{h_{\rho}} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}ilb_{\rho}$. 
    To finish up it suffices to note for a given flat family of substacks 
    $\mathfrak{Z}$ by first forming the associated family of schemes $\Xi$ 
    that $I(\Xi)$ is an admissible ideal with respect to the given 
    $G$-grading and this association is unique. As such the reverse 
    association $\mathfrak{Z} \rightarrow I$ defines an inverse morphism of 
    sheaves to the one constructed above. Finally by Yoneda's lemma there is 
    an induced isomorphism on the fine moduli spaces which is what we wished 
    to prove.
  \end{proof}

title: Lemma
body_md:
There is a natural morphism of stacks $\mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$ which 
    is a homeomorphism on geometric points. 
    \begin{proof}
        As $\mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$ is a rigidification of $\mathcal{X}$ included in this data 
        is a functorial morphism $F: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$. More 
        concretely we will briefly describe its construction.
        To begin, let $T \in Sch/k$. As $G$ is a finite group it is 
        affine so in particular the fiber category $\mathcal{X}(T)$ is equivalent to 
        the groupoid of principal $G$-bundles 
        \[\begin{tikzcd}
        	P & X \\
        	T
        	\arrow["\pi", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
        \end{tikzcd}\]
        where $\pi$ is a $G$-equivariant morphism; Further discussion of this 
        may be found on pages 171-172 of \cite{Olsson_2016}. As $H$ acts 
        trivially with respect to the action on $\mathbb{A}^2$ it is clear the 
        action on families is also trivial. As such we may meaningfully define 
        an action of $G/H$ on principal bundles by the declaration
        $gH \cdot P = g \cdot P$. From here it is easy to see $\pi$ is 
        also a $(G/H)$-equivariant morphism and $F$ is defined by 
        regarding $P$ as a $(G/H)$-bundle with the constructed action.

        Next let $S$ be the coarse moduli space of $\mathcal{X}$ and $S_{\operatorname{rig}}$ the 
        coarse moduli space of $\mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$. As $G$ is finite and $\mathbb{A}^2$ is 
        quasiprojective we have $S = \mathbb{A}^2/G$ and $S_{\operatorname{rig}} = \mathbb{A}^2/(G/H)$
        with their respective actions. Similar to the above argument there 
        is a morphism $f: S \rightarrow S_{\operatorname{rig}}$ and in fact $f$ is an 
        isomorphism. As there is a homeomorphism 
        between the geometric points of a DM stack and its coarse moduli 
        space the final claim follows from the commutativity of 
        \[\begin{tikzcd}
        	\mathcal{X} & {\mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}} \\
        	S & {S_{\operatorname{rig}}}
        	\arrow["F", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        	\arrow["q"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
        	\arrow["{q_{\operatorname{rig}}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
        	\arrow["f"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
        \end{tikzcd}\]
        and the composition of homeomorphisms            
        $\mathcal{X} \rightarrow S \xrightarrow{f} S_{\operatorname{rig}} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$.
    \end{proof}

title: Proposition
body_md:
For all $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G/H)$ there is an isomorphism
$P_{\operatorname{rig}}: \mathcal{X}^{[\rho]} \simeq \mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}^{[\rho]}$.
\begin{proof}
    More concretely, $P_{\operatorname{rig}}$ is given on $T$-valued 
    points $P \to T$ by regarding $P$ as a $(G/H)$-bundle in the 
    same manner as described above. An inverse can be 
    explicitly described. By the quotient $G \rightarrow G/H$, if $P$ is a 
    $(G/H)$-bundle under the constructed action clearly it may also 
    be regarded as a $G$-bundle. Moreso its representation type may be 
    calculated either with respect to $G$ or $G/H$, and this 
    association is functorial. Thus by a functor of points argument 
    there is an induced morphism 
    $Q_{\operatorname{rig}}: \mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}^{[\rho]} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}$. 
    To complete the proof we need only note from their constructions clearly 
    $P_{\operatorname{rig}} \circ Q_{\operatorname{rig}}$ and 
    $Q_{\operatorname{rig}} \circ P_{\operatorname{rig}}$ are the 
    identity morphism on their respective spaces as the underlying bundle 
    is unchanged by both maps.
\end{proof}

label: DeltaRepCase
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{DeltaRepCase}
  Suppose $\mathfrak{z} \subset \Delta$ is a zero dimensional substack. Then 
  $\varrho(\mathfrak{z}) \simeq m \mathfrak{R}$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$. 
  \begin{proof}
    Let $\xi \subset \mathbb{A}^2$ denote the $G$-subscheme corresponding to $\mathfrak{z}$. 
    $\xi_{red}$ decomposes into a disjoint union of free and reduced 
    orbits, $p_i = \operatorname{Orb}_G(x_i)$, for some $x_i$. Let $\xi_i$ denote the 
    maximal subscheme of $\xi$ supported on $p_i$ so 
    $\xi = \bigsqcup_i \xi_i$. As the union is disjoint there is a 
    $G$-isomorphism
    \begin{equation*}
      H^0(\xi) \simeq \bigoplus_i H^0(\xi_i)
    \end{equation*}
    from which the claim follows from the special case of each summand. 
    Hence without loss of generality assume $\xi_{red} = \operatorname{Orb}_G(q)$ for some 
    reduced $q \in \mathbb{A}^2$. Now consider the $G$-isomorphism 
    \begin{equation*}
      H^0(\xi) \simeq \bigoplus_{g \in G} H^0(g \cdot q)
    \end{equation*}
    There are $\# G$ distinct summands since q has a trivial stabilizer.
    If we set $m = h^0(q)$ this implies $h^0(\xi) = m \cdot \#G$.
    Next let $\{f_i\}_{i = 1}^m$ be a basis of $H^0(\xi)$ as a 
    k-vector space and define 
    $$R_i = \bigoplus_{g \in G} \operatorname{Span}(g \cdot f_i)$$ 
    As $g$ acts transitively on $\xi_{red} = Orb_G(q)$, each $R_i$ consists of
    $\# G$ distinct summands. 
    By the association $f_i \leftrightarrow 1 \in \mathfrak{R}$, a 
    dimension count, and comparison of the actions there is an 
    isomorphism of representations $R_i \simeq m_i \mathfrak{R}$ 
    for some $m_i \in \mathbb{N}$. As
    \begin{equation*}
      H^0(\xi) \simeq \bigoplus_{i = 1}^{m} R_i
    \end{equation*}
    and the inclusion of each summand is a $G$-linear map this 
    implies $H^0(\xi) \simeq m \mathfrak{R}$ as representations for 
    $m = \sum_i m_i$.
  \end{proof}

label: AutoRemoval
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{AutoRemoval}
  Let $\sigma_1, \sigma_2: G \rightarrow GL(2)$ be two homomorphisms 
  and assume there exists an automorphism $\varphi \in \operatorname{Aut}(G)$
  such that $\sigma_2 = \sigma_1 \circ \varphi$. Then 
  $\sigma_1 \simeq \sigma_2$.
  \begin{proof}
    The key point is that $G$ is finite so that any automorphism 
    is given by a scheme theoretic isomorphism. More precisely 
    as $G$ is finite it may be represented by the group scheme 
    $\bigsqcup_{g \in G} C_g$ where $C_g \simeq \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C})$ for each 
    $g \in G$ and the group action is given in the usual way. 
    As each automorphism is uniquely determined as a permutation 
    of the components this shows $\varphi$ gives rise to an automorphism 
    of group schemes. Then the action on principal bundles is defined 
    according to the product $G \times P \rightarrow P$ so that $\varphi$
    induces an automorphism of principal bundles. Continuing on in 
    this fashion we may construct a morphism of fiber categories 
    $\mathcal{X}_1(T) \rightarrow \mathcal{X}_2(T)$ which evidently is compatible 
    with base change, and thus we obtain a morphism 
    $\mathcal{X}_1 \rightarrow \mathcal{X}_2$. As $\varphi$ is an automorphism in 
    turn the map of stacks admits an inverse and thus $\mathcal{X}_1 \simeq \mathcal{X}_2$
    from which it is trivial that $\sigma_1 \simeq \sigma_2$.
  \end{proof}

label: DiagEq
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{DiagEq}
  Let $\sigma: G \rightarrow GL(2)$ denote an arbitrary representation with 
  an induced action on $\mathbb{A}^2$. Then there exists $f_{j,i}$ for $j = 1, 2$,
  $i = 1,...,k$ such that 
  \begin{equation*}
    \sigma \simeq (d_1;f_{1,1}, f_{2,1}) \oplus ... \oplus (d_k; f_{1,k}, f_{2,k})
  \end{equation*} 
  \begin{proof}
    Set $\sigma_i: \mathbb{Z}/(d_i) \subset G \rightarrow GL(2)$ where the 
    first arrow is given b $1 \rightarrow e_i$. As isotypic coordinates 
    exist since $G$ is abelian we may simultaneously diagonalize each 
    $\sigma_i$ individually so that 
    $\sigma_i \simeq (d_1;f_{1,i}', f_{2,i}')$ for some parameters. To 
    show the final condition of the definition is met we will argue on 
    induction on $k$. Clearly if $k = 1$ then the claim is true. 
    Now assume we have shown it for all groups with less than $k$ 
    summands, and set $G' \simeq \bigoplus_{i = 1}^{k - 1} \mathbb{Z}/(d_i)$
    with the usual inclusion $G' \subset G$. If $\sigma'$ is 
    the induced representation then by the inductive hypothesis 
    necessarily
    \begin{equation}
      \sigma' \simeq (d_1;f_{1,1}, f_{1,2}) \oplus ... \oplus (d_{k - 1}; f_{1,k-1}, f_{2,k-1})
    \end{equation}
    for some choice of parameters and associated primitive roots of unity 
    $\zeta_{d_i}$. 
    
    On the other hand assume $(d_k;f_{1,k}', f_{2,k}')$
    is given by $e_k \cdot (x,y) = (\omega^{f_{1,k}'} x, \omega^{f_{2,k}'}y)$
    where $\omega$ is a primitive $d_k$-th root of unity. As 
    $\zeta_{d_{k - 1}}$ is itself primitive necessarily there exists 
    primitive $\zeta_{d_{k}}$ such that 
    $\zeta_{d_{k}}^{d_{k}/d_{k - 1}} = \zeta_{d_{k - 1}}$. Now observe 
    there exists a unit $u \in \mathbb{Z}/(d_k)$ such that $\omega = \zeta_{d_k}^u$,
    and set $f_{k,i} = u f_{k,i}'$. At each step we have only applied 
    automorphisms of $G$ in such a way that we obtain equivalent 
    actions. Thus by Lemma \ref{AutoRemoval} we obtain an 
    isomorphism of the corresponding quotient stacks at each step and hence 
    on induction we have proven
    $$\sigma \simeq (d_1;f_{1,1}, f_{2,1}) \oplus ... \oplus (d_k; f_{1,k}, f_{2,k})$$
  \end{proof}

body_md:
\label{CycDoubGenRed}
  Let $\sigma: G \rightarrow GL(2)$ be an arbitrary representation 
  such that associated action on $\mathbb{A}^2$ is not the trivial action. Then 
  either $\sigma \simeq (n; a,b)$ or 
  $\sigma \simeq (m; a,b) \oplus (n;c,d)$ for some choice of parameters.
  \begin{proof}
    By Lemma \ref{DiagEq} we have 
    \begin{equation*}
      \sigma \simeq (d_1;f_{1,1}, f_{2,1}) \oplus ... \oplus (d_k; f_{1,k}, f_{2,k})
    \end{equation*}
    for some choice of parameters. By the previous lemma if $k > 2$ then 
    necessarily some element of $G$ stabilizes $\mathbb{A}^2$. Thus we may pass to 
    the rigidification $[\mathbb{A}^2/(G/H)]$. As an additional consequence of the 
    previous lemma necessarily $G/H$ is generated by at most two summands in 
    Smith normal form. Moreso as $G$ does not have the trivial action 
    we have $G \neq H$ and hence $G/H \neq 0$. If $G/H$ is cyclic then the 
    first claim holds. If $G/H$ is generated by two elements the second 
    claim holds.
  \end{proof}

If $\mathcal{X}$ is rigid and $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]} \neq \emptyset$ then
  $t_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho + \mathfrak{R}) = t_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho) + 2$
  \begin{proof} 
    By assumption there exists $\mathfrak{z} \in \mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}$ and as $\mathcal{X}$ is 
    rigid in addition there exists a simple geometric 
    point $p \in \Delta$ not contained in $\mathfrak{z}$. Let $\xi$ be the subscheme 
    corresponding to $\mathfrak{z}$ and $f$ the subscheme corresponding to $p$ 
    and note from the set up both are disjoint subschemes. Now as $p$ 
    is a nonstacky point in turn $\varrho(f) \simeq \mathfrak{R}$ by Proposition 
    \ref{DeltaRepCase}, and by disjointness we have 
    $\varrho(\xi \sqcup f) \simeq \varrho(\xi) + \varrho(f) = \rho + \mathfrak{R}$.
    Thus there is the equality 
    $t_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho + \mathfrak{R}) = \dim(T_{\mathfrak{z} \sqcup p} \mathcal{X}^{[\rho + \mathfrak{R}]})$.
    As shown above there is an isomorphism of groups 
    \begin{equation*}
      T_{\mathfrak{z} \sqcup p} \mathcal{X}^{[\rho + \mathfrak{R}]} \simeq \text{Hom}^G(I(\xi \sqcup f), H^0(\xi \sqcup f))
    \end{equation*}
    where the Hom is taken as $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$-modules. By disjointness of the 
    subschemes in turn
    \begin{equation*}
      \text{Hom}^G(I(\xi \sqcup f), H^0(\xi \sqcup f))
      \simeq \text{Hom}^G(I(\xi), H^0(\xi)) \oplus \text{Hom}^G(I(f), H^0(f))
    \end{equation*}
    By another application of the tangent vector characterization we can 
    see
    \begin{equation*}
        T_{\mathfrak{z} \sqcup p} \mathcal{X}^{[\rho + \mathfrak{R}]} \simeq T_{\mathfrak{z}} \mathcal{X}^{[\rho]} 
        \oplus T_{p} \mathcal{X}^{[\mathfrak{R}]}
    \end{equation*}
    so that by taking dimensions we obtain the equality 
    $t_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho + \mathfrak{R}) = t_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho) + \dim(T_{p} \mathcal{X}^{[\mathfrak{R}]})$.
    To handle the remaining term we will use that $\Delta$ is open in 
    $\mathcal{X}$ to the dimension may be calculated with the tangent space of 
    $\Delta$ at $p$. With the comments following Proposition 
    \ref{DeltaRepCase} it was also shown
    $\Delta^{[\mathfrak{R}]} \simeq \delta$
    for an open subscheme of $\mathbb{A}^2/G$ consisting of smooth points. In total 
    this implies the last tangent space is two dimensional and thus
    $t_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho + \mathfrak{R}) = t_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho) + 2$.
  \end{proof}

title: Lemma
body_md:
Set $w_G = \sum_{g \in G} e_g$. Then 
  $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(v + w_G) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(v)$ for all $v \in \mathbb{R}[G]$.
  \begin{proof}
    By Lemma \ref{QCons} we have 
    $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(\chi(0) + \mathfrak{R}) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(\chi(0))$. In terms of vectors of 
    $\mathbb{R}[G]$ the previous equality implies 
    $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_0 + w_G) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_0)$ since $e_0$ corresponds 
    to the sheaf $[\mathcal{O}(0)]$.  On the other hand 
    observe $g \cdot e_0 = e_g$ and $g \cdot (e_0 + w_G) = e_g + w_G$
    since $v_G$ is a simultaneous eigenvector of the action with an 
    eigenvalue of 1. Thus $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(g \cdot v) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(v)$
    implies $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_g + w_G) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_g)$. On induction this 
    implies $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_g + n \cdot w_G) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_g)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

    Next let $A$ denote the symmetric matrix associated to $Q_{\mathcal{X}}$.
    By direct calculation we find for any choice of $v$ that 
    $$Q_{\mathcal{X}}(v + w_G) = (v + w_G)^T A (v + w_G) = v^T A v + 2v^T A w_G + w_G^T A w_G$$
    Note $\ell(v) = 2 v^T A w_G$ is linear in $v$. Next substituting 
    $v = e_g + n \cdot w_G$ yields
    $$Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_g + n \cdot w_G) = e_g^T A e_g + 2ne_g^T A w_G + n^2 (w_G^T A w_G)$$
    As $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_g + n \cdot w_G) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(e_g) = e_g^T A e_g$ this 
    implies 
    $2n e_g^T A w_G + n^2 (w_G^T A w_G) = 0$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$. As the 
    equation holds for $n = 1, 2$ in turn this implies 
    \begin{equation*}
      \begin{split}
        0 
        &= (4 e_g^T A w_G + 4 w_G^T A w_G) - 2 \cdot (2 e_g^T A w_G + w_G^T A w_G)\\
        &= 2 w_G^T A w_G\\
      \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    and in turn $\ell(e_g) = 2e_g^T A w_G = 0$ for each $g \in G$. As 
    $\ell$ is linear and zero on a basis in turn $\ell(v) = 0$ for all 
    $v$. Finally we have already shown $w_G^T A w_G = 0$ so that 
    upon substituting these into the above equations we have 
    $$Q_{\mathcal{X}}(v + w_G) = v^T A v = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(v)$$
  \end{proof}

body_md:
Let $A$ denote the matrix associated to $Q$ with respect to 
        $\{e_i\}$. The condition of the hypothesis amounts to the equality
        \begin{equation*}
            v^T A ~v = (v + \overline{1})^T A ~ (v + \overline{1}) = v^T A ~ v + 2 v^T A  ~ \overline{1}+ \overline{1}^T A ~ \overline{1}
        \end{equation*}
        from which we can deduce 
        $2 v^T A ~ \overline{1} + \overline{1}^T A ~\overline{1} = 0$.
        As this holds for all $v$ necessarily 
        $v^T A ~ \overline{1}, \overline{1}^T A ~ \overline{1} = 0$.
        By sampling $e_i$ in the first expression we can 
        see that each row sum of $A$ must be equal to 0, from which the 
        second equality is implied as $A \cdot \overline{1}$ is equal to the 
        vector of row sums. In fact the opposite direction holds as 
        well so the the hypothesis is satisfied iff each row sum of $A$ is 
        equal to 0.

        Next write $A = (b_{i,j})$ and observe 
        \begin{equation*}
        \begin{split}
            \sum_{i < j} -b_{i,j}(a_i - a_j)^2 
            &= \sum_{i = 1}^n \bigg( \sum_{j \neq i} -b_{i,j} a_i^2 + \sum_{i \neq j} 2 b_{i,j} a_i a_j\bigg)\\
            &= \sum_{i = 1}^n \bigg( b_{i,i} a_i^2 + \sum_{i \neq j} 2 b_{i,j} a_i a_j\bigg) = Q(a_1,...,a_n)\\
        \end{split}
        \end{equation*}
        where we have used $\sum_{i = 1}^n b_{i,j} = 0$ in the last equality.
        To see the claim on the coefficients recall $Q_{\mathcal{X}}$ is an 
        integral quadratic form so that $b_{i,j} \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$.

Assume $\dim(\mathcal{C}_g) = 0$. Then 
  $\widetilde{\operatorname{Ch}}([L_x])_g = \chi_{g}(-g_x), \widetilde{\operatorname{Ch}}([L_y])_g = \chi_{g}(-g_y)$.
  \begin{proof}
    For the canonical projection, $q: I \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, 
    there are isomorphisms obtained from pulling back,
    $q^* [L_x]_g \simeq [\mathcal{O}(-g_x)]_g$. Next 
    $\widetilde{\operatorname{Ch}} = \text{Ch} \circ \rho$, where $\rho$ is the eigenvalue map. By 
    comparison the element $g$ acts on $[\mathcal{O}(-g_x)]$ with an eigenvalue of 
    $\chi_g(-g_x)$. As such 
    \begin{equation*}
      \begin{split}
        \widetilde{\operatorname{Ch}}([L_x])_g 
        &= \text{Ch}\big(\rho([\mathcal{O}(-g_x)]_g)\big) \\
        &= \text{Ch}(\chi_g(-g_x) \cdot [\mathcal{O}(-g_x)]_g]) \\
        &= \chi_g(-g_x)\text{Ch}([\mathcal{O}(-g_x)]_g]) = \chi_{g}(-g_x)\\
      \end{split}
    \end{equation*}
    The penultimate equality arises from pulling $\chi_g(-g_x)$ out of 
    $\text{Ch}$ as it is a complex root of unity, and the last equality 
    uses that $c_1([\mathcal{O}(-g_x)] \vert_{\mathcal{C}_g}) = 0$ as $\dim(\mathcal{C}_g) = 0$. 
    The calculation for $L_y$ is identical and will be omitted.
  \end{proof}

        $\widetilde{\operatorname{Td}}([\mathcal{X}]) = \widetilde{\operatorname{Td}}([L_x]^{\vee})\widetilde{\operatorname{Td}}([L_y]^{\vee})$.

        \begin{equation*}

        denominator, clearly

        its dual pulls back to $[\mathcal{O}(g_x)]_g$.

        calculating the remainder of the denominator yields:
        \begin{equation*}
            \begin{split}
                \text{Ch}\big(\rho \circ \lambda_{-1}([\mathcal{O}(-g_x)]_g)\big)
                &= \text{Ch}\big(\rho([\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{C}_g}] - [\mathcal{O}(-g_x)]_g\big)\\

                &= 1 - \chi_g(-g_x) \cdot \text{Ch}([\mathcal{O}(-g_x)_g])= 1 - \chi_g(-g_x)\\

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{EulerFormCoeffs}
    Let $\mathcal{X} = [\mathbb{A}^2/G]$ and $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G)$ satisfy
    $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]} \neq \emptyset$. Then for $a_g = \langle \rho, \chi(g) \rangle$
    we have
    \begin{equation*}
      Q_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho) = 
        \sum_{(g,h) \in D} b_{g,h} (a_g - a_h)^2
    \end{equation*}
    where $b_{g,h} = \frac{1}{2}\langle \rho_{\operatorname{std}} - \chi_c, \chi_{g-h} + \chi_{h-g} \rangle$.
    \begin{proof}
      The above calculations prove the claim when $\mathcal{X}$ is rigid and 
      thus all that remains is to extend to the general 
      case. As such let $H$ denote the stabilizer group of the generic 
      point. Recall the quotient $G \to G/H$ induces an inclusion 
      of groups $\operatorname{Irr}(G/H) \subset \operatorname{Irr}(G)$ by dualizing, and thus 
      we will regard $\operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$ as a subgroup. First note 
      $g_x,g_y,c \in \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$. Furthermore recall if 
      $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]} \neq \emptyset$ then necessarily $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G/H)$. 
      In particular if $a_g \neq 0$ then $\chi(g) \in \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$.
      Now assume $\chi(g),\chi(h) \notin \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$. It follows $a_g, a_h = 0$
      since $\rho \in \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$ and thus $b_{g,h}(a_g - a_h)^2 = 0$.
      On the other hand assume $\chi(g) \in \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$ and 
      $\chi(h) \notin \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$. In this case although it may 
      happen $a_g \neq 0$ observe that $\chi(g - h) \notin \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$ 
      as $\operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$ is a subgroup. As such
      \begin{equation*}
        b_{g,h} = \frac{1}{2} \langle \rho_{\operatorname{std}} - \chi_c, \chi_{g - h} + \chi_{h - g} \rangle = 0
      \end{equation*} 
      since both terms in the left component correspond to representations 
      contained in $\operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$. Thus $b_{g,h} (a_g - a_h)^2 = 0$ in 
      this case as well. In total the only terms which nontrivially 
      contribute to the sum are those when $\chi(g),\chi(h) \in \operatorname{Irr}(G/H)$.
      Finally the equality
      \begin{equation*}
      Q_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho) = \sum_{(g,h) \in D} b_{g,h} (a_g - a_h)^2
      \end{equation*}
      may be established by passing to $\mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$.
    \end{proof}

There is the equivalence of actions $(4;2,2) \simeq (2;1,1)$. Let 
  $\mathcal{X}$ be the quotient stack of the first action and note
  $\mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$ corresponds to the second action. Upon setting 
  $Q_{\mathcal{X}}^{\operatorname{rig}}$ to be the Euler form of $\mathcal{X}_{\operatorname{rig}}$ it is easy to 
  calculate $Q_{\mathcal{X}}^{\operatorname{rig}}(A_0,A_1) = 2(A_0 - A_1)^2$. 
  Upon taking a rigidification the induced 
  $\operatorname{Irr}(\mu_4/\mu_2) \subset \operatorname{Irr}(\mu_4)$ corresponds to the subgroup 
  $(2) \subset \mu_4$ so that $Q_{\mathcal{X}} = 2(a_0 - a_2)^2$. Next set 
  $C(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3) = 2(a_0 - a_2)^2 + 2(a_1 - a_3)^2$.
  Recall that for all $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(\mu_4/\mu_2) \subset \operatorname{Rep}(\mu_4)$ we 
  have $\rho \simeq a_0 \chi(0) + a_2 \chi(2)$. As such if $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}$ 
  is nonempty then clearly $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3) = C(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3)$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
$\mathcal{X}$ is trivial type iff it satisfies one of the 
  three following conditions: (i) $g_x, g_y = 0$,
  (ii) $g_x = 0$ , or (iii) $g_y = 0$ .
  \begin{proof}
    Note that from direct calculation if any of the above conditions 
    hold then necessarily $Q_{\mathcal{X}} = 0$ and so one direction is clear.
    For the other direction now assume $Q_{\mathcal{X}} = 0$ and at least 
    one of $g_x,g_y$ is nonzero. Clearly $Q_{\mathcal{X}} = 0$ iff all 
    coefficients are zero. As $\mathcal{X}$ is rigid, with the natural 
    action of $G$ on $\operatorname{Rep}(G)$ there is the orthogonality relation 
    $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(g \cdot \rho) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho)$ for all $g \in G$.
    Thus if $b_{g,h}$ are the coefficients of $Q_{\mathcal{X}}$ we have 
    $b_{g' + g, g' + h} = b_{g,h}$ for all $g',g,h \in G$ and thus 
    it suffices to consider only the coefficients $b_{g,0}$. Next by 
    Theorem \ref{EulerFormCoeffs} we have  
    $b_{g,0} = \frac{1}{2} \langle \chi_{g_x} + \chi_{g_y} - \chi_{c}, \chi_{g} + \chi_{- g} \rangle = 0$.
    As we have assumed not both of $g_x,g_y$ are zero this implies
    at least one of the characters in the left component 
    of the inner product is not equal to $\chi_{0}$. However if 
    both $\chi_{g_x}, \chi_{g_y}$ were nontrivial then we could choose 
    $g \in \{g_x, g_y\} \subset G$ to obtain a nonzero 
    coefficient. By relabeling if necessary we will assume 
    $\chi_{g_x} = \chi_{0}$. However as $\chi(g_x)$ 
    uniquely corresponds to $\chi_{g_x}$ this implies $g_x = 0$.
  \end{proof}

    one of $g_x,g_y$ is nonzero. Clearly $Q_{\mathcal{X}} = 0$ iff all 
    coefficients are zero. As $\mathcal{X}$ is rigid, with the natural 
    action of $G$ on $\operatorname{Rep}(G)$ there is the orthogonality relation 
    $Q_{\mathcal{X}}(g \cdot \rho) = Q_{\mathcal{X}}(\rho)$ for all $g \in G$.
    Thus if $b_{g,h}$ are the coefficients of $Q_{\mathcal{X}}$ we have 
    $b_{g' + g, g' + h} = b_{g,h}$ for all $g',g,h \in G$ and thus 
    it suffices to consider only the coefficients $b_{g,0}$. Next by 
    Theorem \ref{EulerFormCoeffs} we have  
    $b_{g,0} = \frac{1}{2} \langle \chi_{g_x} + \chi_{g_y} - \chi_{c}, \chi_{g} + \chi_{- g} \rangle = 0$.
    As we have assumed not both of $g_x,g_y$ are zero this implies
    at least one of the characters in the left component 
    of the inner product is not equal to $\chi_{0}$. However if 
    both $\chi_{g_x}, \chi_{g_y}$ were nontrivial then we could choose 
    $g \in \{g_x, g_y\} \subset G$ to obtain a nonzero 
    coefficient. By relabeling if necessary we will assume 
    $\chi_{g_x} = \chi_{0}$. However as $\chi(g_x)$ 
    uniquely corresponds to $\chi_{g_x}$ this implies $g_x = 0$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{GroupConstraint}
  Suppose $G = \mu_n$ or $\mu_m \oplus \mu_n$ with $m \mid n$, and 
  that $\mathcal{X} = [\mathbb{A}^2/G]$ is a rigid stack. If 
  $k \cdot g_x, \ell \cdot g_y = 0$ and $L = \operatorname{lcm}(k,\ell)$ then 
  $n \mid L$.
  \begin{proof}
    In the cyclic case if the action is given by $(n;a,b)$ the hypothesis 
    amounts to requiring $ka, \ell b = 0 \text{ (mod }n)$. On the other hand 
    we can calculate 
    $\zeta^{L} \cdot (x,y) = (\zeta^{aL} x, \zeta^{bL} y) = (x,y)$. As such 
    $\zeta^L$ stabilizes the generic point, but as $\mathcal{X}$ is rigid 
    this implies $L = 0 \text{ (mod }n)$.

    For the doubly generated case form the fundamental matrix.
    As $g_x = (a,c), g_y = (b,d)$ and $L \cdot g_x, L \cdot g_y = 0$
    it follows $(L,L)^T \in \ker(M_G)$. As the action was assumed to 
    be rigid we must have $(L,L)$ is the zero vector 
    and thus $L = 0 \text{ (mod }n)$ as claimed.
  \end{proof}

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Disentanglement}

  $\Xi \subset \mathbb{A}^2 \times T$ be a $G$-flat family over some connected 
  and reduced scheme $T$. $\Xi$ is said to be a disentanglement if there 
  exists a nonempty open subset $U \subset T$ such that for all $t \in U$:
  (i) $\Xi_t = f_t \cup \zeta_t$ with $f_t \in \Delta^{[m\mathfrak{R}]}$ for some 
  $m > 0$ independent of $t$, and (ii) $\zeta_t \in \mathbb{G}_{\rho - m \mathfrak{R}}$.

title: Lemma

    Proposition \ref{GFlatLimit}. Thus $\varrho(\zeta) = \varrho(\xi) - m\mathfrak{R}$. 
    Finally as $Y(\zeta) = Y - B$, the claim that $B$ is regularly colored 
    follows by translating the above calculation into color types of the 
    corresponding diagrams.

label: ExcisableSubsets
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{ExcisableSubsets}
  Let $Y$ be a diagram and $B \subset B(Y)$ be a regularly colored subset 
  such that $Y - B$ is a diagram. Then $B$ is excisable.
  \begin{proof}
    For simplicity we will assume the color type of $B$ is $(1,...,1)$.
    By assumption $Y - B$ is a diagram. Let $\xi$ be the 
    subscheme corresponding to $Y - B$ and $\eta$ the subscheme to $Y$. Let 
    $f = \operatorname{Orb}_G((1,1))$ and set $\Xi_1'(t) = \xi \cup (t \cdot f)$ for 
    $t \in \mathbb{C}^*$ using the standard torus action. It can 
    be verified $\Xi_1'$ is a $G$-flat family. Moreso as $t \rightarrow 0$ 
    the orbit limits to an attracting point, and hence a $G$-flat 
    limit exists. As such the family may be extended to 
    $\Xi_1 \subset \mathbb{A}^2 \times \mathbb{A}^1$ such that $\Xi_1(0) \in \mathbb{G}_{\rho}$.
    
    As $G$-flat limits preserve representation type, necessarily $\Xi_1$ has 
    constant representation type which is isomorphic
    to $\rho = \varrho(\eta)$ so $\Xi'(0) \in \mathbb{G}_{\rho}$. 
    By Propositions 3.10 and 3.12 of \cite{Maclagan_Smith_2010} we know
    $\mathbb{G}_{\rho}$ is rationally connected by using the induced families from 
    positive and negative significant arrows. As such there exists a 
    family $\Xi_2 \subset \mathbb{G}_{\rho} \times C$ for some connected curve 
    curve $C$ which deforms $\Xi_1(0)$ to some $\eta = \Xi_2(t_0)$ so the 
    concatenation $\Xi = \Xi_1 \cup \Xi_2$ is a disentanglement. As 
    $\Xi(t_0) = \eta$ and $\Xi(1) = \xi \cup t \cdot f$ the 
    condition for $B$ to be excisable has been met. 
  \end{proof}

label: RegColoring
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{RegColoring}
    Fix $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a binary sequence $S_i$, let 
    $Y_i$ be the minimal diagram of $S_i$, and set $B_i = B(Y_i)$. Then 
    $B_i$ is regularly colored with respect to $\mathcal{C}_n$.
    \begin{proof}
        The argument will proceed on induction with respect to the 
        number of ones in $S_i$. If $S_i = (0,...,0)$ then 
        $Y_i = \{(i,0) \mid 0 \leq i \leq n - 1\}$ from which the claim 
        is easily verified. Next choose $i \neq 2^{n - 1} - 1$, 
        form $Y_i$ and choose $j$ such that $c_j$ is the last entry of 
        $S_i$ which is zero. Consider the sequence $\mathfrak{f}_j^{+}(S_i)$. 
        By giving $B_i = \{p_k\}$ a linear order as above we can define 
        $B_i^* = \{p_k^*\} \subset \mathbb{N}^2$ by setting $p_k^* = p_k$ if 
        $k < j$, and $p_k^* = p_k - (1,1)$ if $k \geq j$. 
        After changing $0$ to $1$ in the sequence it may be the case
        $p_i^*$ has negative coordinates. 
        
        To circumvent this recall that the 
        coloring is a semigroup homomorphism $\mathcal{C}_n: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mu_n$
        and thus may be extended to a homomorphism 
        $\mathcal{C}_n: \mathbb{Z}^2 \rightarrow \mu_n$. Note the extension also 
        satisfies $\mathcal{C}_n(i,j) = \mathcal{C}_n(i + N, j + N)$ for all $N \in \mathbb{Z}$. As 
        such $\mathcal{C}_n(p_k^*) = \mathcal{C}_n(p_k)$ for all $k$ so $B_i$ and $B_i^*$ 
        have the same color type. On the other hand by forming 
        $\mathfrak{f}_j^{+}(B_i)$ from $\mathfrak{f}_j^{+}(S_i)$ it is not hard to see 
        $\mathfrak{f}_j^{+}(B_i) = B_i^* + v$ for some $v \in \mathbb{Z}^2$. As the effect of 
        translations on the color type is to permute the coordinates 
        necessarily $B_{i}^*$ is regularly colored iff $\mathfrak{f}_j^{+}(B_i)$ is 
        regularly colored. Finally since $\mathfrak{f}_j^{+}(S_i)$ 
        has less zeroes than $S_i$ by our inductive hypothesis 
        $\mathfrak{f}_j^{+}(B_i)$ is regularly colored, whence $B_i$ is as well.
    \end{proof}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{BorderPush}
    Suppose $(i;u,v) \in T_i(M)$ and $(u+1, v+1) \in Y$. Then 
    $(i; u+1, v+1) \in T_i(M)$.
    \begin{proof}
        Note $\mathcal{C}_n(u+1, v+1) = \mathcal{C}_n(u,v) = \mathcal{C}_{n}(p_i, q_i)$
        and hence $(i; u+1, v+1)$ is an arrow of $M$. Next, 
        since $u < u + 1$ and $v < v + 1$ it follows 
        $0 \leq (i; u, v) \leq (i; u+1, v+1)$. Now assume 
        $(i;u,v) \in T_{\geq 0}(M)$. In particular $i > 0$ and 
        $(u + p_{i - 1} - p_i, v) \notin Y$. As $Y$ is a diagram clearly 
        $(u + 1 + p_{i - 1} - p_i, v + 1) \notin Y$.

label: ShaftLength
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ShaftLength}
    Let $w = (i; u,v)$ be a nonnegative arrow of $Y$. If $S$ is a shaft of 
    $w$ then $n \mid \ell(S)$.
    \begin{proof}
      Similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{RegColoring} we can apply a 
      seequence of positive and negative flips to $S$ to obtain an arrow 
      either of the form $(i; 0,v)$ or $(i;u,0)$ and shafts $S_q, S_p$ 
      defined below. In the first case there is a unique shaft of 
      the arrow $S_q = \{(p_i, q_i - i)\}$ and necessarily $v < q_i$. Since 
      $\mathcal{C}_n(p_i, q_i) = \mathcal{C}_n(u,v) = \mathcal{C}_n(p_i, v)$ this implies 
      $q_i = v \text{ (mod }n)$ so $q_i = v + kn$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$; By comparison it 
      is easy to see $\ell(S) = kn$. In the second case define 
      \begin{equation*}
          S_p = \{(0,q_i - j) \mid 1 \leq i \leq q_i\} \cup \{(j,0) \mid 1 \leq j \leq n\}
      \end{equation*}
      Along the first column the shaft passes through $(0,v)$ and thus it 
      suffices to show $n \mid u + v$ since this is equal to the number of 
      squares between both points. As 
      $\mathcal{C}_n(u,0) = \mathcal{C}_n(p_i,q_i) = \mathcal{C}_n(0,v)$ necessarily 
      $u + 0 = 0 - v \text{ (mod }n)$. Upon rearranging 
      $u + v = 0 \text{ (mod }n)$, as $u, v \geq 0$ this implies 
      $u + v = k'n$. Thus $\ell(S_p) = kn + k'n$ so $n \mid \ell(S_p)$. 
      Finally as every shaft of $(i;u,v)$ has a length equal to either 
      $\ell(S_q)$ or $\ell(S_p)$ this implies $n \mid \ell(S)$ for all 
      $S$.      
    \end{proof}

title: Proposition
body_md:
For $0 < i < m$, if $Y$ is an $n$-core then $T_i(M) = \emptyset$. 
    \begin{proof}
        The assumption $0 < i$ is not restrictive since by definition a 
        nonnegative significant arrow must satisfy $0 < i$.
        Assume there exists $(i; u,v) \in T_{\geq 0}(M)$ with $0 < i < m$ so 
        there is an arrow between $(p_i, q_i)$ and $(u,v)$. As 
        $(p_i - p_{m - 1}, q_{i})$ is a minimal square not contained in $Y$ 
        and $\mathcal{C}_n(p_i, q_i) = \mathcal{C}_{n}(u,v)$, necessarily 
        $\mathcal{C}_n(p_i - p_{m - 1}, q_i) = \mathcal{C}_n(u - p_{m - 1}, v)$ so 
        $(i; u - p_{m - 1}, v)$ is an arrow of $Y'$.   
        Furthermore the arrow is nonnegative as $u \geq p_i$ implies 
        $u - p_{m - 1} \geq p_i - p_{m - 1}$. It can be verified
        $x^{u + p_{i - 1} - p_i} y^v \in M$ implies 
        $x^{u - p_{m - 1} + p_{i - 1} - p_i} y^v \in M'$. As such
        $(i; u - p_{m -1}, v) \in T_{\geq 0}(M')$ 
        which contradicts $T_{\geq 0}(M')$. Hence 
        $(i;u,v)$ cannot exist so $T_i(M) = \emptyset$.
    \end{proof}

title: Proposition
body_md:
If $Y$ is an $n$-core then $T_m(M) = \emptyset$.
    \begin{proof}
        Note if $w \in T_m(M)$ then necessarily $w = (m; u,v)$ for some 
        $(u,v) \in Y$. By Lemma \ref{BorderPush} assume 
        $(u,v) \in B(Y)$ and define a shaft of $(m;u,v)$ by 
        \begin{equation*}
          S = \{(i, q_{m} - 1) \mid 0 \leq i \leq u\} \cup \{(u, q_{m} - i) \mid 1 \leq i \leq q_m - v\}
        \end{equation*}
        Let $k = \min\{j \in \mathbb{N} \mid x^{p_k} y^v \in M\}$. 
        If $p_k = u + 1$ then $S$ is a hook of $(0,v)$ so 
        $n \mid \ell(S)$ by Lemma \ref{ShaftLength} which implies $(0,v)$ is 
        an $n$-hook. This contradicts the assumption that $Y$ is an $n$-core
        so necessarily $p_{k} > u + 1$. As the arrow is significant and 
        nonnegative, it is the case $x^{u + p_{m-1}} y^v \in M$ so 
        $p_k \leq u + p_{m - 1}$. Hence $p_k - u \leq p_{m - 1}$. 
        
        Next let $S'$ be the translation of $S$
        by the vector $(p_k - u,0)$. If $(i, 0) \in S$ then 
        $i \leq q_{m}, p_k - u \leq p_{m - 1}$ so $(i,p_k - u) \in Y$ for all 
        such $i$. Similarly $(i + p_k - u, v) \in Y$ for all $i$ in the 
        horizontal leg. In total $S + (p_k - u, 0) \subset Y$. 
        Moreso this translates the shaft so the
        uppermost and rightmost legs are contained in the border. Hence 
        $S'$ is the hook of $(p_k - u, v)$. Translating preserves the length
        so $\# S' = \ell(S)$. By Lemma \ref{ShaftLength} in turn 
        $S'$ is an $n$-hook which contradicts the assumption $Y$ is an 
        $n$-core. Thus $(m;u,v)$ cannot exist so $T_{m}(M) = \emptyset$.
    \end{proof}

label: NumBorderStripFormula
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{NumBorderStripFormula}
  Let $Y \subset \mathbb{N}^2$ be a Young diagram colored by $\mathcal{C}_n$. Then $t_n(Y)$
  is equal to twice the number of border strips which can be removed before 
  obtaining an $n$-core. 
  \begin{proof}
    If $Y$ is an $n$-core then by the above equivalences it is also a 
    $G$-core. As such $t_n(Y) = 0$ from which the claim is vacuously true. 
    Assume without loss of generality $Y$ is not a $G$-core so it is not a 
    $B$-core and hence there exists an excisable border strip $B \subset Y$. 
    Let $(a_0,...,a_{n-1})$ be the color type of $Y$. The color type of 
    $Y-B$ is $(a_0 - 1, ..., a_{n - 1} - 1)$ as $B$ is regularly colored. 
    By the substituting the color type of $Y - B$ into the formula for 
    $t_n$ and simplifying the resulting expression it follows 
    $t_n(Y - B) = t_n(Y) - 2$. Set $B_1 = B$. 
    
    If $t_n(Y - B_1) > 0$ the same argument may 
    be repeated to construct $B_2 \subset Y - B_1$. Repeat these steps
    until $t_n(Y - \bigcup_i^k B_i) = 0$. As $G = B$ upon reaching this 
    step no more excisable border strips remain. On induction it can be 
    calculated $t_n(Y - \bigcup_i^k B_i) = t_n(Y) - 2 k$ for all $k$. 
    Thus taking the largest possible index and setting the equations 
    equal to each other yields $t_n(Y) = 2k$.
  \end{proof}

title: Proposition
body_md:
There exists a bijection
\begin{equation*}
  \{n\text{-core partitions}\} \leftrightarrow \{(a_0,...,a_{n - 1}) \in R_n \mid 2a_0 = \sum_i (a_i - a_i)^2\}
\end{equation*}
\begin{proof}
      Let $p_1 \geq ... \geq p_m$ be an $n$-core partition and $Y$ be the 
      associated Young diagram with color type $p = (a_0, ..., a_{n - 1})$.  
      Define a map to $\mathbb{N}^n$ by sending $Y$ to $p$. This is well defined as 
      each partition gives rise to a unique diagram. 
      As $n=G$ it follows $t_n(Y) = 0$ so that in particular
      \begin{equation*}
        2 a_0 = \sum_i (a_i - a_{i + 1})^2
      \end{equation*}
      As such the image of the above map is contained in $R_n$, and from its 
      definition the map is necessarily surjective. 
      To show injectivity we need to show $n$-core diagrams are uniquely 
      determined by their color types. 
      
      To see this, let 
      $\rho \simeq \sum_i a_i \chi(i)$. As $t_n(Y) = 0$ it follows 
      $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}$ is zero dimensional. Since Gilbert schemes are 
      quasiprojective in turn $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}$ is a finite collection of 
      points. By Proposition 3.12 of \cite{Maclagan_Smith_2010} they are 
      also connected and hence $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}$ is a singleton. In particular 
      if $\xi$ is the monomial subscheme corresponding to $Y$ then 
      $\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]} = \{\xi\}$ from which it is easily seen the map is 
      injective.
\end{proof}

title: Proposition
body_md:
2-cores are in a bijective correspondence with all solutions of 
  $2a_0 = 2(a_0 - a_1)^2$.
  \begin{proof}
    We will omit the calculation that solutions of the equation are given 
    by $(j^2, j^2 \pm j)$ for $j \in \mathbb{N}$. Now let $b \in \{0,1\}$ and 
    define $Y_{j,j - b}$ to be the diagram corresponding to the partition 
    $(2j - b) + ... + 1$. In all cases $j$ counts the number of antidiagonals 
    of white squares. It can be verified the $i$-th antidiagonal has $2i - 1$ 
    squares so in total there are $j^2$ white squares. If $b = 0$ then there 
    are $j$ antidiagonals of black squares, of which the $k$-th one has 
    $2k$ squares. Thus there are $2 + ... + 2j = j^2 + j$ black squares 
    in $Y_{j,j}$ whence its color type is $(j^2, j^2 + j)$. The case 
    $b = 1$ is virtually identical and will be omitted. In particular 
    $(j^2, j^2 \pm j) \in R_2$ for all $j \in \mathbb{N}$, which is what we wanted 
    to prove.
  \end{proof}

body_md:
M = 0 iff $\mathcal{D}_n^{[\rho]}$ is a singleton. Furthermore, 
  its unique point is a monomial subscheme $\xi$ such that $Y(\xi)$ 
  is a core diagram.
  \begin{proof}
    The first claim is immediate since $M = \dim(\mathcal{D}_n^{[\rho]})$ and 
    $\mathcal{D}_n^{[\rho]}$ is connected by Theorem 1.1 of 
    \cite{Maclagan_Smith_2010}. For the second claim, choose 
    $\xi \in \mathcal{D}_n^{[\rho]}$. As Grobner deformations induce $G$-flat 
    families it follows $\text{in}(\xi) \in \mathcal{D}_n^{[\rho]}$ for any 
    admissible monomial order. However Grobner deformations are 
    parameterized by $\mathbb{A}^1$ so as $\mathcal{D}_n^{[\rho]}$ is a singleton we 
    have $\xi = \text{in}(\xi)$, i.e., $\xi$ is a monomial subscheme.
    Finally $Y = Y(\xi)$ is a core diagram as 
    $t_n(Y) = \dim(\mathcal{X}^{[\rho]}) = 0$.
  \end{proof}

body_md:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\rho \in \operatorname{Rep}(G)$, and 
  $\rho_{\operatorname{min}} = \rho - M \mathfrak{R}$ be the minimal core of $\rho$. 
  There is a partition $\mathcal{D}_n^{[\rho]} = \bigsqcup_{k = 0}^M O_k$ such that 
  $O_M = \mathbb{G}_{\rho_{\operatorname{min}}} \times \Delta^{[M\mathfrak{R}]}$. Furthermore
  the elements of the partition are connected smooth varieties and are in a 
  bijective correspondence with diagrams of size $\deg(\rho - k\mathfrak{R})$ colored by 
  $\mathcal{C}_n$.
